name: Esther Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Oh, my days start before the sun. I buy fresh produce and imported foods for Calloway Fresh Wholesale, down by the docks in Portsby: plantain, yams, peppers, spices, dried fish for about two hundred African and Caribbean grocers. I'm on the phone with importers and growers by six, and I'm at the market floor twice a week to touch the fruit myself. I use an AI tool now and then to compare price lists or translate a message. What wears me out is the pay, which is lower than it should be for the risk I carry, because when a container sits at the port I'm the one who answers for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, all right, good, don't panic. At work I'd tell people to keep using the tools for the boring bits and keep their eyes open. With friends at church I'd say, nothing new under the sun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's quiet on the AI front but it's not quiet at home. We have a mortgage, Abena is thirteen and Kwesi is nine, and we have less than a month saved. Kofi works as a pharmacy technician, so we're steady, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and use AI for translating and price lists, since it saves me time. I'd try to save a little more for the roof, which is leaking in the back bedroom. I'd also ask Mr Calloway for a review, because the tomatoes and the stress have both gone up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Sort of grateful. But when the roof leaks, you don't feel grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In a quiet world where AI changes little, what pressures does your household still have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roof, honestly. A quote came in at three thousand. If Kofi's hours drop, or a container is lost, we couldn't pay for it. So I call it a quiet world, but my own life has plenty of noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your boss to do differently if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a proper bonus when I save the firm money on a bad shipment, instead of a thank you. Last year I rescued a delayed container of peppers and nobody said a word. A small share of what I save would change my attitude.

say: I'd say **don't panic**, keep using the tools for boring bits and stay alert.
I'd tell friends at church there's **nothing new** under the sun.
think: It's quiet on AI but **not at home**: the mortgage, two children and under a month saved.
Kofi's pharmacy pay keeps us **steady, just**.
do: Use AI for **translating** and price lists to save time.
Save for the **leaking roof**, quoted at three thousand.
Ask Mr Calloway for a **review** or a bonus for rescued shipments.
feel: **Okay**, a bit grateful; but a leaking roof is hard to feel grateful about.
S0.quote: I call it a quiet world, but my own life has plenty of noise.
fieldNote: Home costs, not AI, decide her mood; the **roof** is the concrete worry.
Wants her **risk** recognised with a bonus.
Uses AI for **small chores**, which fits her steady adaptability.

steps.text: Use the AI tool to translate supplier messages and compare price lists
Put aside a hundred a month for the roof repair
Ask Mr Calloway for a bonus on every rescued shipment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario two is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we should expect it, and we should prepare for it. At work I'd tell the team that the ones who learn the tools will stay. At church I'd talk about looking after those who lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried but not hopeless. Price comparison, order planning and booking deliveries are all on that card, and I do them every day. But what I really do is trust. The growers pick up my call because they know me, and that's harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools more, properly, and ask the boss to send me on a supply chain course. I'd also save for six months of expenses. I'd make myself the person who handles the growers and the problems, because software can't ring a farmer at night and calm him down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sad. I like my work as it is, with all its mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks do you think software takes first, and which would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reorder planning goes first, and the paperwork for the port. Calloway already has a new system for invoices that the finance team loves. After that, price comparison. I'd hold on to the grower relationships and the problem solving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you see the change first at Calloway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office team, I think, because the invoices are what they do. For me it's a longer road, but I'm not special. If the firm needs two buyers and not four, I'd want to be one of the two, and I'd have to earn that.

say: I'd say **expect it** and prepare, and the ones who learn the tools will stay.
I'd talk at church about **looking after** those who lose out.
think: Price checks and order planning are on that card, but my real skill is **trust** with growers.
do: Use the tools **properly** and ask for a supply chain course.
Become the person who handles **growers and problems**.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit sad; I like my work with all its mess.
S1.quote: The growers pick up my call because they know me, and that's harder to replace.
fieldNote: Believes **trust with growers** is her protection, since buying is partly a relationship job.
Admits she is **not special** and would have to earn a place.
Practical steps: **a course** and a cushion.

steps.text: Use AI for price comparison and port paperwork every week
Ask the boss to fund a supply chain course
Save toward six months of expenses in a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario three is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is a huge shock, and we need leaders who tell the truth. I'd tell people at work to prepare, and I'd say at church that we should help each other. Online I'd stay quiet, because it's too big for a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be afraid. If AI can do almost any thinking work, I don't see how a buyer stays. We have no savings, no space to retrain without income, and not many wholesale buyer jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my family and my church community early, because that's where help is. I'd sit down with Kofi and work out what we can cut. I'd apply for whatever public support exists, and I'd talk to the growers about selling directly. If the container trade stays with people, I could run my own small import brokerage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel it in my chest on the way to work. But I'd also pray and try to keep my head clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what do you do in the first six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could take courses and save. With two, I have to find money and a role at the same time. I'd use the first months to find my feet and ask for help, which I'm not used to doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job is desk and phone with market visits. How does the three-year gap before robots matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots after three years doesn't do much for me, since most of my work is a phone and a laptop. It might help the market floor, where hands are needed. But the buyer's chair is the first one to go, and I'd have to think about the floor, the docks or a small business of my own.

say: I'd say this is a **huge shock** and we need leaders who tell the truth.
I'd say at church that we should **help each other**.
think: If AI does almost any thinking work, I **don't see** how a buyer stays.
We have **no savings** and not many buyer jobs nearby.
do: Go to **family and church** for help early.
Work out what **we can cut** with Kofi and apply for public support.
Talk to growers about a small **import brokerage** of my own.
feel: **Alarmed**, felt in my chest on the way to work, but praying to stay clear.
S2.quote: With ten years I could take courses and save. With two, I have to find money and a role at the same time.
fieldNote: Turns to **community and faith** first, a real support network.
Sees a **brokerage** idea as a long shot built on her grower trust.

steps.text: Ask family and the church community for help with childcare and bills
Cut the household budget with Kofi, starting with takeaways and subscriptions
Offer to broker imports for two small grocers on commission
Apply for warehouse and logistics supervisor jobs by the docks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario four is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, five years is a window, so let's use it. I'd tell people at work to start learning now, and at church I'd talk about caring for neighbours. I'd also say the government should get its plans ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but with some hope. Five years lets me take the supply chain course, save, and build a small business on the side. It's not guaranteed, but it's a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the supply chain certificate and set up a small brokerage on evenings and Saturdays for two grocers I trust. I'd save every spare cedi, I mean coin, for the roof and a cushion. I'd also learn the AI tools properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I like having a plan, even a rough one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What do you do differently in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the world might need people who understand people and things you can touch. I'd tell Abena to study something she's curious about, not just what looks safe. I'd tell Kwesi to be kind and to keep reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to Abena and Kwesi about work in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The surprising thing is that five years makes me braver. I'd probably have started the brokerage anyway, because buyers always dream of working for themselves. A deadline just gives me permission.

say: I'd say five years is a **window**, so let's use it.
I'd say the **government** should get its plans ready.
think: I'd be anxious but with **hope**; five years lets me finish a course and save.
do: Finish the **supply chain** certificate in year one.
Start a small **brokerage** on evenings and Saturdays for two grocers.
feel: **Anxious** but with a plan, even a rough one.
S3.quote: I'd probably have started the brokerage anyway, because buyers always dream of working for themselves.
fieldNote: The extra time makes her **braver**, not just safer.
Her plan rests on **people she trusts**, grocers and growers.
Wants her children to choose **curiosity** over safety.

steps.text: Finish the supply chain certificate by next summer
Broker imports for two trusted grocers on weekends
Use AI every week for price comparison and contracts
Save a hundred a month for the roof and a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario five is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but we have time, so let's be sensible. At work I'd keep using the tools and learning. At church I'd say, plan, but don't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. By 2036 I'm fifty-three, and I'd have time to build something. The worry is that my life now has plenty of bills, and I can't let a future problem eat today's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and learn the tools better each year. I'd do the course part-time over a few years. And I'd probably start a small brokerage when the kids are older, so there's something to land on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A little restless, because I can feel the clock, but it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is this still on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Calloway for training time on the clock. And I'd ask the government to make sure training is paid for, and that people don't fall into the gap. It's about fairness, but also plain sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your boss or the government to do in this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's on my mind. But the money stress is now, and the tech stress is later. I'd put today's bills first and tomorrow's plan second.

say: I'd say it's big but there's **time**, so let's be sensible.
At church I'd say **plan**, but don't lose sleep.
think: I'm fine; by 2036 I'd have **time to build** something.
I can't let a **future problem** eat today's money.
do: Keep my job and **learn the tools** better each year.
Do the course **part-time** over several years.
Start a small **brokerage** when the kids are older.
feel: **Pretty calm**, a little restless as I can feel the clock.
S4.quote: The money stress is now, and the tech stress is later.
fieldNote: Long time lets her **prioritise** present bills over the future.
Asks for **training on company time**, a pragmatic request.
Stays **uneasy**, as the date is far but the household budget is not.

steps.text: Ask Calloway for training time on the clock each month
Study the supply chain course part-time over three years
Save fifty a month toward the children's studies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to prepare. I'd feel the whole house shake. What would help is training paid for while you still have a wage, notice from the firm, and a way for neighbours and the church to help each other. And some honesty from leaders. Tell us the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think buyers just click on a screen. The job is knowing who to trust, and who's lying about a container. I hope that counts for something if the screens get cleverer.

headlineQuote: People think buyers just click on a screen. The job is knowing who to trust, and who's lying about a container.
portrait: **Esther Mensah**, 43, buys fresh and imported foods for Calloway Fresh Wholesale in Portsby, on **lower pay** with under a month saved.
Her **partner Kofi** is a pharmacy technician; they have two children, a mortgage and a leaking roof.
She uses AI now and then and believes **trust** with growers is her protection.
Her mood runs from **uneasy** to **alarmed** in the 2028 world, and she leans on family, church and a small brokerage plan.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because there's no time to train, save and build a plan together.
whatWouldHelp: **Training** paid while she still has a wage, early notice, and **honest** leadership.
